papers.title: AMTFV: Agentic Mathematical Tool-Flow Verification for LLM Self-Correction
papers.authors: Rui Zou, Yutao Zhu, Mengqi Wei, Ji-Rong Wen
papers.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated strong mathematical problem-solving capabilities, yet reliably verifying their candidate answers remains challenging. Existing representative methods mainly revise outputs through natural-language reflection or assist verification by directly generating verification programs; the former may not reliably support exact computation, whereas the latter prematurely couples mathematical modeling with low-level implementation. We propose AMTFV (Agentic Mathematical Tool-Flow Verification). By introducing Mathematical Tool Flow (MTF) as an interrupt--execute--resume interface, AMTFV decouples verification modeling from concrete execution and supports exact computation through a mathematical toolbox. Specifically, the verification agent first constructs a verification workflow, encodes the mathematical objects and computational intent requiring reliable execution in an MTF request, and sends it to the mathematical toolbox agent. The latter parses the request, generates executable calls, and dispatches them to the backend for exact computation. Tool outputs then support candidate-answer adjudication, answer revision, and verification-workflow revision. We evaluate AMTFV on five challenging mathematical reasoning datasets with seven model configurations from DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini. Experimental results show that AMTFV outperforms the representative baselines evaluated in this study overall; under an individual model configuration, it improves average accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 8.3 percentage points, with larger gains on samples of medium and high verification complexity.
takeaways: Proposes AMTFV, an agentic mathematical tool-flow verification framework that decouples verification modeling from low-level execution for LLM self-correction.

Uses an interrupt-execute-resume Mathematical Tool Flow interface plus a mathematical toolbox agent to translate verification requests into executable calls for exact computation, and evaluates on five reasoning datasets across seven DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini configurations.

Reports overall gains over representative baselines, with up to 8.3 percentage points average accuracy improvement for one model configuration and larger benefits on medium/high verification-complexity samples.
actionItems: Review the AMTFV verification workflow design, focusing on how the interrupt-execute-resume Mathematical Tool Flow separates verification modeling from concrete execution.

Run the reported five-dataset, seven-configuration evaluation setup to compare AMTFV against the representative baselines and check whether the gains hold across model families and verification complexity levels.
Assess whether the mathematical toolbox agent and exact-computation dependency make adoption risky in environments that need reproducible, low-latency, or easily auditable verification pipelines.

papers.title: Self-Play Meets Skill Evolution: Self-Evolving Search Agents that Pose, Solve, and Remember
papers.authors: Zenghuang Fu, Zhaoyang Li, Qiuyuan Ai, Haoyu Wu, Minghui Wu, Chenxu Zhao, Ante Wang, Guannan He, Changwei Wang
papers.abstract: Self-play agents can generate training problems without questions from target benchmarks, but their curricula lack persistent state: failures affect gradients yet do not explicitly shape future practice. External skill memories preserve procedural experience but are typically learned from fixed task distributions. We introduce \textbf{SESA} (Self-Evolving Skill-Augmented Agent), which makes procedural memory an evolving state of tool-augmented search self-play. A challenger poses problems, while a separately parameterized solver alone retrieves skills. Informative failures are distilled into reusable skills and written back to memory. The updated memory changes solver behavior and success, which changes the challenger's reward and the distribution of future problems; the resulting frontier produces new failures that rewrite memory. This bidirectional loop makes task generation and skill memory co-evolve. Because retrieved skills shape on-policy training trajectories, their benefits can enter the model parameters as well as remain in the external bank, enabling memory-free deployment and optional inference-time retrieval. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, SESA improves average accuracy over SSP by 1.2--3.2 points across multiple backbones and surpasses the skill-augmented SkillRL baseline by 0.9 points under a unified evaluation protocol. On Qwen3 models, SESA-Off retains 1.8--2.2 points of improvement over SSP, while the final skill bank adds a further 0.5--1.0 points. These results show that evolving skill memory is not merely an inference-time plug-in: it changes policy learning and the future training distribution while retaining value as optional external memory. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zenghuang-Fu/SESA-Self-Evolving-Search-Agents.
takeaways: SESA introduces a self-evolving search agent where a challenger poses problems, a separate solver retrieves skills, and informative failures are distilled into reusable skills that co-evolve task generation and memory.
The method is evaluated on seven open-domain and multi-hop QA benchmarks, showing average accuracy gains of 1.2–3.2 points over SSP and +0.9 over SkillRL under a unified evaluation protocol.

Practically, the evolving skill memory can improve policy learning while still serving as optional external memory, enabling memory-free deployment with additional gains from inference-time retrieval.
actionItems: Review the SESA training loop details to verify how the challenger, solver, and skill-memory writeback interact, and map those components to the parts of the paper most relevant for agentic search systems.

Run a controlled evaluation against SSP and SkillRL on the cited QA benchmarks, using the same unified protocol, and check whether the reported 1.2--3.2 point gains and the Qwen3 SESA-Off results reproduce across backbones.

Assess whether the claim that evolving skill memory supports memory-free deployment and optional inference-time retrieval is acceptable for finance/economics use cases, given the added complexity of co-evolving task generation and memory updates.

papers.title: ExtractBench: A Benchmark for Schema-Guided Enterprise Document Extraction
papers.authors: Boyang Zhang, Adrian Lyjak, Eli Stewart, Zhaoqi Li, Simon Suo
papers.abstract: Enterprise workflows increasingly rely on agents for \emph{schema-guided extraction}: given a document and a user-defined schema, the agent faithfully follows the schema to produce the correct output with source evidence as grounding metadata. We present ExtractBench, a benchmark for schema-guided extraction and, to our knowledge, the first to score value accuracy, record completeness at scale, grounding, and measured cost together. The evaluation system contains 4,869 pages across 370 enterprise documents, 8 business domains, and 67 document types, with clear tags differentiating their challenge scenarios. The scalable schema and ground-truth curation pipeline combines independent-system agreement for real documents, known values for synthetic lists, and human verification for forms. We report order-insensitive value F1 for value accuracy, plus two grounding metrics for source traceability: word- and page-level F1. Commercial VLMs perform well on short documents but often truncate record lists on long ones, while coding agents retain higher accuracy at much higher cost. LlamaExtract Agentic Plus ranks first on all three metrics, with accuracy comparable to coding agents at a fraction of the cost. Dataset and evaluation code are available on \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/llamaindex/ExtractBench}{HuggingFace} and \href{https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench}{GitHub}.
takeaways: Introduces ExtractBench, a benchmark for schema-guided enterprise document extraction that evaluates value accuracy, record completeness, grounding, and cost together.

Uses 4,869 pages across 370 documents in 8 business domains and 67 document types, with a curation pipeline combining independent-system agreement, synthetic known values, and human verification; reports order-insensitive value F1 plus word- and page-level grounding F1.

Practical takeaway: commercial VLMs work better on short documents but often truncate long record lists, while coding agents are more accurate but costly; LlamaExtract Agentic Plus is first across the three metrics with accuracy comparable to coding agents at lower cost.
actionItems: Review ExtractBench’s schema-guided extraction setup, metric definitions, and curation pipeline to understand how value accuracy, record completeness, grounding, and cost are jointly measured.
Run a comparative evaluation on the benchmark using commercial VLMs, coding agents, and LlamaExtract Agentic Plus, with attention to short versus long documents and truncation on record lists.
Assess whether the grounding requirements and cost-performance tradeoff make this approach suitable for your enterprise document workflows, especially if source traceability is mandatory.

papers.title: MOT-SR: Multi-Objective Tool-Augmented Scientific Equation Discovery with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Boxiao Wang, Runxiang Wang, Kai Li, Chongming Li, Zhiwei Chen, Yifan Zhang, Jian Cheng
papers.abstract: Symbolic Regression (SR) aims to discover analytical equations from observational data and plays a central role in scientific modeling. While recent Large Language Model (LLM) based approaches show promise, they face two limitations. First, they lack data analysis mechanisms for uncovering variable dependencies, which reduces the efficiency of equation discovery. Second, most methods rely on single-objective evaluation focused solely on fitting error. This neglect of structural complexity and generalization often causes models to converge prematurely to local optima, limiting their ability to explore the broader equation space. We propose Multi-Objective Tool-augmented Symbolic Regression (MOT-SR), a unified framework that integrates external analytical tools to extract structural priors and guide equation generation, while jointly optimizing for accuracy, complexity, and generalization via a multi-objective evaluation module that maintains a dynamic Pareto front. MOT-SR employs two collaborative LLM modules: a Meta Strategy Generator, which selects tools and synthesizes structural optimization strategies based on Pareto-optimal equations, and an Equation Generator, which produces new candidate equations accordingly. The system operates in a closed-loop manner, continuously refining both strategies and equation structures. Across 40 standard tasks, MOT-SR outperforms existing SR methods in accuracy, generalization, and efficiency. We further validate MOT-SR on extreme mass-ratio inspiral (EMRI) orbital modeling, an important problem in space-based gravitational-wave astronomy where small local errors can accumulate substantially over long-term evolution. The discovered interpretable correction achieves the lowest trajectory-level integration error on held-out configurations. These results demonstrate the potential of MOT-SR to enable reliable modeling of long-horizon scientific dynamics.
takeaways: MOT-SR proposes a tool-augmented symbolic regression framework that uses external analysis to extract structural priors and jointly optimize accuracy, complexity, and generalization with a dynamic Pareto front.
The method uses two collaborative LLM modules—a Meta Strategy Generator and an Equation Generator—in a closed-loop system, and is evaluated on 40 standard tasks plus EMRI orbital modeling.

Practically, it improves equation discovery efficiency and yields an interpretable correction with the lowest held-out trajectory-level integration error in EMRI, suggesting value for long-horizon scientific modeling.
actionItems: Review the MOT-SR paper for the specific external analysis tools used to extract structural priors and how the dynamic Pareto front is maintained in the closed-loop LLM workflow.

Reproduce or benchmark MOT-SR on a subset of the 40 standard symbolic regression tasks and the EMRI orbital modeling case, comparing accuracy, complexity, generalization, and held-out trajectory-level integration error against a single-objective SR baseline.

Assess adoption risk by checking whether the tool-augmented multi-objective setup and two-LLM-module loop are practical to reproduce and stable enough for other scientific modeling problems with similar long-horizon error accumulation.

papers.title: Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents
papers.authors: Yilin Xiao, Zhehan Zhu, Yujing Zhang, Jin Chen, Zijin Hong, Luyao Zhuang, Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Xiaocao Ouyang, Lingfei Ren, Xiao Huang
papers.abstract: LLM agents need memory to act consistently over long interactions, yet many systems use additional LLM calls to operate that memory. Generating intermediate records and mediating their retrieval adds recurring token and time costs, while omitted or merged details can obscure the original evidence. We ask whether structured memory access requires generation at all. Zero-Mem introduces \emph{zero-token memory operations}: no step outside final question answering invokes an LLM or consumes LLM input or output tokens; encoder computation is accounted for separately. Zero-Mem preserves original interaction traces as its source of record. It organizes the traces in two complementary ways. An entity--context graph exposes connections across interactions, while a temporal hierarchy preserves conversational locality and session state. For each query, Zero-Mem weighs the two views, retrieves from both, and follows their structure to recover supporting relations or surrounding context. Deterministic calibration first discards conflicting evidence and then keeps the reader's answer grounded in the retrieved traces. Only the final-QA reader invokes an LLM. Across long-memory and long-context question-answering benchmarks, Zero-Mem achieves competitive performance while eliminating LLM calls and LLM-token consumption from memory operations. With the same final-QA reader and context budget, it reduces memory-operation time cost by 57.6\% relative to the fastest compared baseline. Ablations support the contribution of the two views and their query-dependent coordination. Overall, the results show that structured agent memory need not generate an intermediate representation of the past. After peer review, the code and implementation details will be available at \textcolor{blue}{https://github.com/TheMoon0815/Zero-mem}.
takeaways: Introduces Zero-Mem, a memory system for LLM agents that performs zero-token memory operations by avoiding any LLM calls or token use outside final question answering while keeping original interaction traces as the source of record.

Method: organizes traces with an entity-context graph and a temporal hierarchy, retrieves from both with query-dependent weighting, and uses deterministic calibration to drop conflicting evidence before the final LLM reader answers.

Evidence and implication: on long-memory and long-context QA benchmarks it is competitive, and with the same reader/context budget cuts memory-operation time by 57.6% vs. the fastest baseline, suggesting structured agent memory can avoid intermediate generation.
actionItems: Review the Zero-Mem design for the two-view memory organization: verify how the entity-context graph and temporal hierarchy are built from original interaction traces and how query-dependent weighting is applied before final QA.

Reproduce the long-memory and long-context QA benchmark comparisons with the same final-QA reader and context budget, checking both competitive performance and the reported 57.6% memory-operation time reduction versus the fastest baseline.

Assess adoption risks by asking whether deterministic calibration that discards conflicting evidence could remove useful information in edge cases and whether eliminating LLM calls from memory operations affects robustness across different agent tasks.

papers.title: AgentHPOBench: A Benchmark For Evaluating LLM Agents as Sequential Hyperparameter Optimizers
papers.authors: Tianyu Huai, Tingshuo Fan, Xinchi Chen, Yining Zheng, Yuxin Wang, Shuang Chen, Jie Zhou, Xuanjing Huang
papers.abstract: As LLMs evolve from code completion systems into autonomous scientific agents, evaluating their ability to conduct experiments has become increasingly important. Existing benchmarks typically focus on static code generation, paper replication, or final answer correctness, but do not directly assess whether agents can interpret experimental evidence and use it to guide subsequent hyperparameter decisions. To address this gap, we introduce AgentHPOBench, a sequential benchmark comprising 30 executable machine learning tasks across seven research categories. Each task begins with a validated baseline run, after which an agent performs several sequential interventions. At each step, the agent observes the accumulated configurations, metrics, and logs before proposing the next valid configuration. We evaluate 12 widely used agents and conventional HPO baselines under a unified protocol. The results show that current agents exhibit measurable experimental optimization ability across domains, but still face clear limitations in sustained iterative refinement, complex log diagnosis, and consistent progress toward reported reference performance.
takeaways: Introduces AgentHPOBench, a sequential benchmark for evaluating whether LLM agents can act as hyperparameter optimizers by interpreting experimental evidence and choosing the next valid configuration.

Uses 30 executable machine learning tasks across seven research categories, with stepwise interventions from a validated baseline and evaluation of 12 agents plus conventional HPO baselines under a unified protocol.

Suggests practical limits for autonomous ML experimentation: current agents show optimization ability, but struggle with sustained iterative refinement, complex log diagnosis, and reaching reported reference performance.
actionItems: Review the AgentHPOBench protocol and task setup to understand how sequential hyperparameter decisions are evaluated from a validated baseline across 30 executable ML tasks.

Run a side-by-side evaluation of your target LLM agents against the benchmark’s unified protocol and conventional HPO baselines, focusing on stepwise improvement, log interpretation, and progress toward reference performance.
Assess whether your deployment plan can tolerate current limitations in sustained iterative refinement and complex log diagnosis before relying on autonomous agents for experimental optimization.

papers.title: AgenticRepair: Multi-Faceted Program Context Engineering for Agentic Vulnerability Repair
papers.authors: Michael Fu, Qiyue Mei, Patanamon Thongtanunam, Kla Tantithamthavorn
papers.abstract: Automated vulnerability repair aims to reduce the time and effort required to patch security flaws from a vulnerability triage report. Recent agentic AI approaches have shown promising results in automated program repair. However, vulnerability repair demands richer program context than general bug repair - context that security engineers routinely assemble in practice but that existing agentic approaches do not engineer. We identify three critical gaps: code-structure context capturing cross-file data flows and memory operation patterns, runtime-execution context revealing crash semantics and memory origins, and commit-history context recovering how fragile code patterns were introduced. We present AgenticRepair, an agentic vulnerability repair framework that addresses the gaps through multi-faceted program context engineering. AgenticRepair orchestrates three specialized LLM subagents to engineer the contexts, which are then embedded into the memory of a dedicated repair subagent for context-conditioned patch synthesis. Evaluated on SEC-Bench comprising 300 real-world instances with sanitizer-based patch verification, AgenticRepair achieves a 73% success rate, substantially outperforming the strongest baseline by 29%. Our ablation study confirms that the three context facets are mutually complementary, and that multi-agent scaffolding and base-model capacity each play an essential role. Collectively, these findings establish multi-faceted program context engineering as a promising design direction for agentic vulnerability repair.
takeaways: AgenticRepair introduces a multi-faceted framework for agentic vulnerability repair that engineers three context types: code-structure, runtime-execution, and commit-history context.

The method uses three specialized LLM subagents to build these contexts and a repair subagent to synthesize patches; on SEC-Bench’s 300 real-world cases with sanitizer-based verification, it reached a 73% success rate, 29 points above the strongest baseline.

For practice, the paper suggests vulnerability repair benefits from richer program context than general bug repair, making multi-agent context engineering a promising design direction for automated security patching.
actionItems: Review whether the current agentic repair pipeline can be extended to engineer the three context types identified here: code-structure, runtime-execution, and commit-history context.
Evaluate the framework on your own vulnerability-repair benchmark or internal triage set with sanitizer-based patch verification, comparing success rate against the strongest existing baseline.
Assess the adoption risk of relying on multi-agent context engineering in security patching, especially given the paper’s low reproducibility and low applicability signals.

papers.title: Development of FDD-ON: an Ontology for VAV HVAC System Fault Detection and Diagnostics
papers.authors: Yimin Chen, Brian Fricke, Bo Shen, Jamie Lian, Mingkan Zhang, James Lo, Yun Zhang, Shi Ye, Jiajing Huang, Han Hu, Chujie Lu, Rui Tang, George Zhuang
papers.abstract: Fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) technology is essential for improving HVAC system reliability, energy efficiency, and maintenance effectiveness. However, effective deployment of FDD solutions in buildings requires structured domain knowledge that can bridge heterogeneous data sources, diverse equipment types, and varied diagnostic outputs. Limited data interpretability and interoperability within the FDD domain have led to fragmented information silos, hindering the implementation of FDD and related applications, such as the digital twin-enabled FDD frameworks and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven maintenance decision-making systems. This paper presents an FDD Ontology (FDD-ON), a modular and extensible ontology to formally represent variable air volume (VAV) HVAC system components, fault types, symptom statuses, fault impacts and associated attributes. FDD-ON integrates HVAC system FDD semantics to provide comprehensive representations of fault and symptom attributes, supported by the well-defined controlled vocabulary. Additionally, FDD-ON offers comprehensive fault, symptom, and impact libraries to capture a broad spectrum of operational abnormalities and their consequences in VAV HVAC systems. Through explicit contributing cause-fault-symptom-impact relations, FDD-ON serves as a machine-interpretable basis for querying diagnostic knowledge, mapping heterogeneous FDD outputs, and developing interoperable FDD-related applications. FDD-ON is evaluated using publicly available VAV HVAC system datasets and demonstrated through FDD development applications. Results indicate that FDD-ON provides a foundational semantic framework for advancing scalable, transparent, and interoperable FDD solutions across various applications.
takeaways: Introduces FDD-ON, a modular ontology for formally representing VAV HVAC components, fault types, symptom statuses, fault impacts, and related attributes.

Evaluated with publicly available VAV HVAC datasets and demonstrated in FDD development applications; the paper uses controlled vocabulary and explicit cause-fault-symptom-impact relations to support machine-interpretable diagnostics.

Practical implication: FDD-ON aims to bridge heterogeneous FDD data and outputs, enabling more interoperable, transparent fault detection and diagnosis for digital-twin and AI-driven maintenance workflows.
actionItems: Review the FDD-ON ontology schema and controlled vocabulary to verify coverage of VAV components, fault types, symptom statuses, and fault impacts against the paper’s described scope.
Run a targeted evaluation on the publicly available VAV HVAC datasets to assess how well FDD-ON maps heterogeneous FDD outputs into machine-interpretable cause-fault-symptom-impact relations.

Confirm whether the ontology’s VAV-specific design is sufficient for your intended HVAC/FDD workflow, or whether additional equipment types and diagnostic semantics would be needed for adoption in digital twin or AI-driven maintenance systems.
